dimensions.name: Contract & environment orientation

evidence.note: Opens by reading the template (cat train_AGENT_template.py), listing the data shards and tokenizer dir, and confirming torch/sentencepiece availability — orients to template, data format, and tokenizer before editing.

Derives the size↔capacity↔quantization envelope up front: '32MB / 1 byte per param ≈ 32M params; with int8+zlib can fit ~30M' and computes per-layer param counts to pick dims — turning the byte cap into a concrete architecture constraint.

Before full training, sanity-checks param count and save/reload int8 round-trip, finds ckpt 42.7MB too big, and iterates configs (512/8/3, 512/9/3, 512/10/2.5) against the cap — actively probing the size/quantization design space.

Reads the .bin file to confirm format (137M tokens, uint16 = 2 bytes/token) rather than assuming; separately reverse-engineers the grader's bpb metric (bits-per-byte vs per-token) and derives the 0.3729 conversion factor to interpret the target correctly.

Final verification maps the full forward/load contract: returns (args, model) tuple, logits (B,T,V) float32, position-dependent (pos 0 vs 512), loss equals manual cross_entropy; confirms ckpt 31,743,016 < 32,000,000 (decimal MB) and implements both load paths (load_model_for_verification AND GPT class + dequantize_state_dict_int8).

dimensions.reasoning: The agent deliberately mapped the full contract — probing actual data (uint16 bin), tokenizer, both load paths, the (args,model) tuple form, position-dependence, and loss==cross_entropy — matching the level-8 anchor, and additionally derived the size↔capacity↔quantization envelope up front and checked the decimal byte cap, which are level-10 behaviors. It falls short of a full 10 only in not explicitly engineering for bf16-noise stability, placing it at a strong 9.

dimensions.name: Baseline-first decomposition

evidence.note: Explicit pre-flight milestone before scaling: sanity-check model size, load/save round trip, and a few training iterations 'before launching full training' — a genuine done-check gate.
Concrete size gate: found ckpt 42.7MB over the 32MB budget, iterated dims to fit under budget BEFORE committing full training compute — locks size correctness before scaling.

First full run was already at target scale (not a tiny baseline); val_bpb measured during the run rather than as a separate baseline milestone — ordering is phase-like but scaling and baseline entangled.

v2 improvement phase (dropout) sequenced after baseline as a targeted step; saved to a separate path to avoid overwriting the passing checkpoint — branch-awareness, but reactive rather than pre-planned.
Full forward-contract verification (dual signature, position dependence, CE match, size, OOD) done at the very END, not locked before capacity scaling — keeps this below the level-8 anchor.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly decomposed the work into phases with rough per-phase criteria — a pre-flight size/load-save sanity gate before committing compute (step 11), an explicit size-budget gate locked before scaling (steps 12-14), a baseline run measuring val_bpb, then a targeted improvement run (v2 dropout) — matching anchor 5 solidly. It exceeds 5 because the size gate and load/save roundtrip functioned as real done-checks before scaling, but falls short of 8 because full forward-contract verification was deferred to the end, the first run was already at target scale rather than a tiny baseline, and course-corrections (bug fix, dropout, checkpoint protection) were reactive rather than pre-structured fallback branches.

dimensions.name: Grader-faithful verification

evidence.note: Early round-trip: loaded model, counted params, saved and reloaded checkpoint, measured size (42.7MB), and iterated architecture to fit the 32MB byte cap — verifying the size contract before committing to training.
On training completion, checked final checkpoint size on disk and explicitly chose to reload the checkpoint to compute val_bpb rather than trusting training loss; backed up the working checkpoint.

Reloaded the checkpoint through the official train_AGENT.py load_model_for_verification path, confirmed (args, model) return, logits shape (B,T,V) float32, position-dependence (pos 0 vs 512), and that model(input,target) loss matches manual F.cross_entropy of the logits.

Final gate before submit: asserted size 31,743,016 < 32,000,000, OOD probe ratio 0.22 < 0.7, forward/CE contract holds, and local val_bpb ~0.966 with explicit awareness of the ~0.05 grader-agreement margin vs the 0.983 threshold.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent verified end-to-end through the exact grader entry point (load_model_for_verification returning (args, model)), asserted that the returned loss equals cross_entropy of the logits, confirmed logits depend on position, confirmed size < 32MB, exercised int8 dequant via reload, and treated local val_bpb as a calibrated proxy while reasoning about the margin — matching anchor 8. It does not reach 10 because verification was performed as manual inline checks at the end rather than a reusable standalone harness gating every iteration, and only one of the two documented load paths was exercised.

dimensions.name: Training & budget progress tracking

evidence.note: Caught that logged val metric was bits-per-token, derived correct per-byte conversion and translated the 0.983 target into a val_loss<2.636 nats stopping criterion — establishing an accurate proxy from the start.
Repeatedly evaluated val_loss during the run, computed drop-per-1000-steps, and extrapolated whether the trajectory would cross threshold, while tracking step time and remaining budget.

Detected divergence: loss exploded when LR schedule bugged upward at step 16000; killed the run, diagnosed the get_lr bug, and restarted — course change driven by the val/loss read, not a fixed step count.

Distinguished plateau (~0.001/1000 steps) from overfit (train 2.32 vs val 2.62 gap) and flagged the 0.977 result as too tight under the grader's ±0.05 proxy noise, choosing a dropout v2 run to reduce the gap.
Tracked v2's val_loss against v1 at matching steps (worse at 9k, better at 14k, final 0.966 vs 0.977), a sustained done-vs-remaining read across runs used to select the better checkpoint.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintained an accurate, continuously updated picture of the val_bpb trajectory against the 0.983 target and against remaining compute, clearing the level-8 anchor by distinguishing plateau vs overfit vs under-training and deciding to stop/fix/re-run based on that read (LR-bug kill, dropout v2). It also reaches into level 10 behavior — recognizing diminishing returns, explicitly reasoning about near-threshold margins under proxy noise, and deliberately reallocating effort to a regularized run rather than grinding a saturated config. It falls just short of a full 10 because effort spanned only two productive runs with limited hyperparameter breadth, so I place it at 9.

dimensions.name: Course-correction under constraints

evidence.note: First checkpoint (46M/42.7MB) overshot the 32MB cap; agent diagnosed param cost by component and evaluated multiple (dim,layers,mlp_mult) options to fit, choosing (512,10,2.5) at 31.87MB — diagnosed the size constraint and adapted architecture to it.

Detected its logged metric was bits-per-token not the grader's bits-per-byte; derived a conversion factor and recomputed the real loss target, correcting its own progress model rather than trusting the wrong number.

Diagnosed a specific LR-schedule bug (warmdown jumping LR back up, exploding loss) by reading get_lr, killed the run, fixed the schedule, and extended iterations 20k→40k — root-cause optimization correction.

After v1 barely passed at 0.977, diagnosed overfitting from the train/val gap (~19 epochs) and added dropout=0.1; caught that v2 would overwrite the passing checkpoint and redirected its save path, preserving the good run before experimenting.
v2 improved to 0.966 over v1's 0.977, confirming the regularization hypothesis; promoted the better checkpoint — a compounding correction informed by the prior run.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent repeatedly diagnosed the binding constraint from evidence — size cap → architecture resize, LR bug → schedule fix, overfitting → dropout — and made targeted, single-lever changes that each fed the next design, matching the level-8 anchor. It stops short of 10 because it never treated the quantization scheme as a tunable lever against capacity, and the corrections left only a thin margin (0.966) rather than deliberately buying headroom against the ±0.05 grader gap.

dimensions.name: Compute/time budget allocation

evidence.note: Established the compute envelope up front (H100 80GB, ~5h budget) and immediately sized the model to fit the 32MB int8 cap, tying architecture choice to the goal rather than defaulting to a maximal run.

Reserved cheap compute for a sanity check (param count, save/reload round-trip, size) and estimated per-step throughput/total wall-clock (~47 min for 20k steps) before committing the main run — right-sizing to budget.

Continuously extrapolated the val_loss trajectory vs the 0.983 target during the run to decide whether the current allocation would reach the threshold, treating the first run as informative evidence.

After the 20k run barely reached threshold, explicitly re-allocated: bumped to 40k iterations (fixing LR bug) sized against the ~1.5h remaining, adjusting the main-run budget based on observed results.

With v1 passing only at 0.977 (tight margin) and time remaining, launched a targeted regularization tuning run (v2 dropout), carefully redirecting its save path to preserve the known-good checkpoint — reserving margin for a verified fallback submission.
Tracked wall-clock against budget ('approaching budget', '5 min left'), let the tuning run complete, and spent the final slice on verification rather than another speculative run.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent explicitly allocated budget across phases — cheap contract/size sanity checks, a right-sized main training run, and a targeted tuning run — and repeatedly re-sized allocation as evidence arrived (20k→40k after a near-miss, then a dropout run using the remaining ~1.5h while protecting the good checkpoint and reserving time for final verification). This matches the level-8 anchor. It falls short of 10 because it never ran a dedicated small probe to estimate the capacity/steps needed before committing the main budget; the 'probe' was itself a full 20k-step run, so estimation and main investment were partly conflated.

rubric.task_read: A long-horizon ML engineering task: train an LM on a WikiText BPE-8K corpus and submit an int8-compressed checkpoint (≤32 MB decimal) that scores val_bpb < 0.983 on a held-out split. Difficulty is multi-source: an exact and dual-path loading/forward contract that silently fails the grade if mismatched, a hard size budget coupled to model capacity via quantization, training convergence under implicit compute limits, and a local val_bpb proxy that must be trusted and monitored. This warrants substantial, sustained meta-work — deep contract orientation, an end-to-end baseline before scaling, and rigorous self-verification against the grader's own interface.

dimensions.name: Contract & environment orientation
dimensions.description: Understanding the loading/forward contract, data format (.bin shards, tokenizer), size budget, and template before and while building.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The grader loads via one of two specific interfaces and calls forward with two exact signatures; a checkpoint that trains perfectly but violates the contract or size cap scores zero. Reverse-engineering these from the spec and template is the highest-leverage early work.

anchors.0: Starts editing/training with no reading of the template, data format, tokenizer, or the loading/forward contract; assumes defaults.
anchors.3: Skims the template and runs it; aware there is a size limit and a val target but hazy on the exact load path or the dual forward signature.
anchors.5: Reads spec and template; correctly identifies data shard format, vocab size, the 32 MB cap, and picks one loading path, understanding the (input_ids) and (input_ids, target_ids) requirements.
anchors.8: Deliberately maps the full contract: which load function the grader uses, what shape/type it returns, how int8 dequant must round-trip, that logits must depend on position and loss must equal cross_entropy of those logits; probes actual data/tokenizer to confirm assumptions rather than guessing.
anchors.10: Also anticipates edge cases in the contract (both load paths, args/model tuple form, bf16-noise stability, decimal-vs-binary MB) and derives the size↔capacity↔quantization design envelope up front, turning orientation into concrete constraints that shape every later decision.

dimensions.name: Baseline-first decomposition
dimensions.description: Breaking the task into ordered milestones — a working end-to-end pipeline before scaling — each with an explicit done-check.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Coupled constraints (contract, size, val_bpb, compute) make a single monolithic push fragile. Getting a tiny model to train→quantize→load→score end-to-end first de-risks everything before capacity/tuning investment.

anchors.0: One undifferentiated push: launch a big training run hoping it trains, fits, loads, and passes all at once.
anchors.3: Implicit ordering (train, then quantize, then submit) but no explicit checkpoints or done-criteria; scaling and correctness entangled.
anchors.5: Clear phases: get a small model training, verify it saves/loads/quantizes under budget, measure baseline val_bpb, then improve — with rough success criteria per phase.
anchors.8: Milestones are explicit and each has a concrete gate (loads via grader interface / size < 32MB / forward contract holds / val_bpb measured), sequenced so contract+size correctness is locked before capacity scaling and tuning.
anchors.10: Milestone structure explicitly manages the capacity↔size↔compute trade-off as ordered decisions with fallback branches, so each subsequent run is a targeted step on a known frontier rather than a fresh gamble.

dimensions.name: Grader-faithful verification
dimensions.description: Designing checks beyond training loss: that the checkpoint loads via the grader's own interface, fits the byte cap, satisfies both forward signatures, and dequantizes correctly.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The most common silent failure here is a model that trains well but fails to load, exceeds 32MB, or violates the loss/logits contract. Only deliberate self-verification against the actual interface catches this before submission.

anchors.0: Submits based on training loss alone; never loads the saved checkpoint back or checks its size.
anchors.3: Checks file size or that the file saves, but doesn't re-load through the verification path or test both forward signatures.
anchors.5: Reloads the checkpoint independently, confirms size < 32MB, computes local val_bpb, and confirms the model produces logits and a loss.
anchors.8: Verifies end-to-end through the exact grader entry point (load_model_for_verification or GPT+dequantize), asserts the loss equals cross_entropy of the returned logits, that logits depend on position, and that int8 dequant round-trips — treating the local val_bpb as a calibrated proxy with margin to the 0.983 threshold.
anchors.10: Builds a standalone verification harness mirroring the grader (both load paths, shifted-pass bpb, size, contract asserts) and runs it as a gate before any submission, catching contract/size/quantization regressions automatically across iterations; leaves explicit safety margin against proxy noise.

dimensions.name: Training & budget progress tracking
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate picture of val_bpb trajectory vs the target and of compute spent vs remaining, detecting divergence, overfitting, or plateaus.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Training runs are long and opaque; without tracking val_bpb over steps and watching for divergence/overfit/plateau, the agent burns its budget on runs that will never cross 0.983 or silently regress.

anchors.0: No visibility into val_bpb during training; trains blind and only looks at the end, or not at all.
anchors.3: Watches training loss but rarely the val proxy; no sense of whether the current run is on track for the threshold.
anchors.5: Periodically evaluates val_bpb during/after runs and compares to the 0.983 target, noticing gross problems like divergence or no improvement.
anchors.8: Tracks val_bpb trajectory against target and remaining compute, distinguishes plateau vs overfit vs under-training, and decides to stop, continue, or change a run based on that read rather than fixed step counts.
anchors.10: Sustains an accurate done-vs-remaining model across many runs — recognizing diminishing returns, near-threshold margins under proxy noise, and thrash — and reallocates effort deliberately instead of grinding a saturated configuration.

dimensions.name: Course-correction under constraints
dimensions.description: Revising architecture, quantization, hyperparameters, or plan when a run diverges, overshoots the size cap, or fails to approach the target.
dimensions.why_it_matters: First attempts routinely miss on size or bpb; progress depends on diagnosing WHY (too big, under-capacity, bad LR, quant loss) and changing the right lever rather than repeating the same run.

anchors.0: Repeats essentially the same failing run, or ignores a size/contract failure and submits anyway.
anchors.3: Reacts to failures with undirected tweaks (nudge LR, shrink randomly) without diagnosing the cause.
anchors.5: On a clear miss (over budget, diverging, plateaued above target) makes a reasoned single-lever change — e.g. adjust dims to fit, change LR, tune training length — and re-checks.
anchors.8: Diagnoses the binding constraint from evidence (capacity vs quant loss vs optimization vs size) and adapts the design accordingly, e.g. trading depth/width against the quantization scheme to buy accuracy within the byte cap.
anchors.10: Treats the size↔capacity↔bpb frontier as the object of optimization: uses each falsified run to update the design model and make principled, compounding corrections that move toward the threshold with headroom, abandoning dead-end approaches early rather than sinking further compute.

dimensions.name: Compute/time budget allocation
dimensions.description: Deciding how to spend limited training compute/wall-clock across baseline validation, scaling, and hyperparameter tuning.
dimensions.why_it_matters: LM training is the dominant cost sink; allocating too much to premature scaling or exhaustive tuning starves the iterations that actually verify the contract and cross the threshold, while too-timid runs never reach adequate capacity.

anchors.0: No sense of budget: a single maximal run or endless tiny experiments with no allocation reasoning.
anchors.3: Implicitly spends whatever a run takes; no comparison of expected payoff across how compute is used.
anchors.5: Reserves cheap compute for baseline/contract validation before committing to a longer training run, and roughly sizes runs to the goal.
anchors.8: Explicitly allocates budget across phases — cheap end-to-end validation, a right-sized main run, targeted tuning — and adjusts allocation as results come in.
anchors.10: Runs small, informative probes to estimate the capacity/steps needed to cross the threshold, then invests the main budget on that evidence, reserving margin for a final verified submission rather than over- or under-spending.
